# Results — Study 42 (Last-Call): the turn-of-the-month effect, 1950–2026

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Daily returns of the **S&P 500 (^GSPC,
price-only — the index level pays no dividends, which is fine for a TOM-vs-rest difference and is
stated rather than mislabelled)** 1950–2026 for the effect, **SPY (auto-adjusted = total return)**
1993–2026 for the tradable run, and the **^IRX 13-week T-bill** for the cash leg. Turn-of-the-month
= the [-1, +3] window (last trading day of a month + first three of the next), held **exactly** —
the window is a pure function of the exchange calendar, known ex ante, so no signal lag applies.
As-of **2026-06-11**; ^GSPC inputs fingerprint `54fd9e780da2`, SPY `d824e220dbca`.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `REAL` · Tradability `MIRAGE` · "Still alive?" `FADED`

The concentration is **real and large**: on the S&P 500, the four turn-of-the-month days (≈19% of all
days) earned **11.0 bp/day** against **1.9 bp/day** the rest of the time — a Welch t of **5.1** across
76 years. But it is `MIRAGE` to *trade*, even on an rf-consistent footing: a long-the-window book on
SPY with its cash leg **credited at the T-bill** compounds **5.5% a year against buy-and-hold's
10.8%**, and its excess-of-cash Sharpe (**0.41** gross, 0.35 at 2 bp) still trails buy-and-hold's
**0.51** — you forfeit half the return to sit in cash 81% of the time, and 12 round-trips a year of
costs only widen the gap. And the effect has `FADED`, now as a tested claim rather than an assertion:
the TOM premium fell from **11.7 bp/day pre-2008 (t = 6.3)** to **0.6 bp/day since (t = 0.1)** — a
decline that is itself significant (change t = **2.3**). A textbook anomaly that is real, uneconomic,
and arbitraged away.

## Data stamp

- **Effect**: S&P 500 (^GSPC, price-only) daily, 1950-01-03 → 2026-06-11, **19,232 days**
  (3,672 TOM + 15,560 rest), fingerprint `54fd9e780da2`
- **Tradable**: SPY (total return) daily, 1993-02-01 → 2026-06-11, fingerprint `d824e220dbca`;
  cash leg = ^IRX/252

## The effect is real and large

| | mean return | n days |
|---|---|---|
| turn-of-the-month days ([-1,+3]) | **11.0 bp/day** | 3,672 |
| all other days | **1.9 bp/day** | 15,560 |
| every day | 3.7 bp/day | 19,232 |

Welch t for the difference: **5.1**. The ~19% of days in the window carry the lion's share of the
market's drift — this is not noise, it's one of the most replicated calendar facts in finance.

## …and yet trading it loses to buy-and-hold (SPY, 1993–2026)

The book holds exactly the [-1,+3] days — including day −1, the richest day of the effect, which is
tradable because the window is calendar-known before the month begins. Off-window the book earns the
T-bill, and the honest Sharpe race is **excess-of-cash on both sides** (raw Sharpe would flatter the
window book for the 81% of days it banks the cash rate — an rf-inconsistent comparison, not an edge):

| | CAGR | Sharpe (raw) | Sharpe (excess) | max-DD | time in market |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TOM-only, 0 bp | +5.5% | 0.72 | **0.41** | −18% | 19% |
| TOM-only, 2 bp | +5.0% | 0.66 | 0.35 | −18% | 19% |
| TOM-only, 5 bp | +4.3% | 0.57 | 0.26 | −18% | 19% |
| **Buy & hold SPY** | **+10.8%** | 0.64 | **0.51** | −55% | 100% |

A higher *per-day* return doesn't make a strategy: out of the market four-fifths of the time, the
TOM-only book compounds half as fast, and once the cash credit is stripped back out (excess vs
excess) its Sharpe trails buy-and-hold too — before costs. The shallow drawdown is the usual
exposure-reduction illusion ([Study 41](../../41-hangover/)), not risk skill.

## …and it has faded since it was published — tested, not asserted

| | TOM days | non-TOM days | Welch t (slice) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1950–1987 | **13.8 bp** | 0.7 bp | 6.2 |
| 1988–2007 | 11.4 bp | 2.3 bp | 2.6 |
| 2008–on | **4.8 bp** | 4.1 bp | **0.1** |

Formal sub-period test (Welch, premium = TOM − rest): **11.7 bp/day pre-2008 → 0.6 bp/day 2008-on**;
the *decline itself* is significant (t = **2.3**), and the modern premium is statistically zero
(t = **0.1**). McConnell & Xu (2008) documented the effect's strength; the years since show the
McLean–Pontiff fade in one of its cleanest forms.

## The honest takeaway

The turn-of-the-month effect is a `REAL`, large, decades-robust seasonal — and a `MIRAGE` to trade:
even with its cash leg paid the T-bill and the window held without a lag, the book compounds half of
buy-and-hold and trails it on excess-of-cash Sharpe, costs erode the thin edge further, and the
premium has `FADED` to statistical zero since ~2008. A beautiful fact that does not pay.
